question: How should exploratory actions be chosen so that least-squares confidence intervals are uniformly small over an action set?

limits: Exploration-design only: the chapter does not give a bandit algorithm or regret bound itself (see Ch. 22).
Exact optimal integer allocation is 'likely an intractable exercise in integer programming'; the n_a rule is a rounding-up approximation.
Algorithms for infinite action sets are 'much heavier and less practical'; no practical method given.
Estimator is unregularised and requires the chosen actions to span R^d; actions are fixed, not adaptive.
No experiments; Exercise 21.7 asks the reader to implement Frank-Wolfe.
practices: Use a G-optimal (equivalently D-optimal) design as a non-adaptive exploration schedule when the action set is finite (p2, Eq. 21.3).
Settle for an approximate design with g <= (1+eps)g*; exactness is not needed (Note 2).
Compute the design with Frank-Wolfe/Wynn updates, using rank-one updates of V(pi)^-1 for speed (Note 3, Ex. 21.7).
Pick the Frank-Wolfe step size by exact line search gamma_k = (d||a_k||^2 - 1)/(d(||a_k||^2 - 1)) (Eq. 21.8, as printed in text).

a design that minimises g; G stands for 'globally optimal'

figures.caption: The minimum volume centered ellipsoid containing a point cloud. The points on the boundary are the core set. The ellipse is E = {x : ||x||^2_{V(pi)^-1} = d}, where pi is an optimal design.
figures.why: Shows geometrically why a few boundary points (core set) suffice to cover all actions
